planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container stock in early spring or fall into moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil; this old European cultivar grows naturally into a narrow cone without shearing, making it a slow, long-lived substitute for clipped topiary cones or Italian cypress in cooler climates.

directions: Pyramidalis is a classic English boxwood selection that ascends naturally into a dense, narrow cone rather than the rounded mound typical of the species, retaining that silhouette with only minimal touch-up pruning over decades of growth. Small, dark blue-green leaves cover the plant densely from base to tip, giving strong year-round architectural presence as a specimen or paired flanking an entry. Growth is very slow, so plants are best purchased at the size desired; provide afternoon shade in hot summer climates and watch for boxwood leafminer and root rot in poorly drained soil. Its formal conical form has made it a long-standing substitute for clipped Italian cypress or arborvitae cones in traditional garden design.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Boxwood Cultivars

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in spring or fall spaced for a continuous screen; this vigorous, large-leaved English boxwood cultivar is among the hardiest and most wind-tolerant forms, historically favored for tall estate hedges and windbreaks.

directions: Handsworthiensis is a robust, upright English boxwood selection with noticeably larger, glossier leaves than typical B. sempervirens, giving it a coarser but denser texture well suited to large-scale hedging. It is among the most cold-hardy and wind-firm of the sempervirens cultivars, historically planted as tall screens and windbreaks on exposed sites in the British Isles and the American Northeast. Its vigorous upright growth tolerates repeated hard shearing, making it a dependable choice where a tall, opaque evergreen hedge is needed faster than slower dwarf cultivars can provide. Give it good drainage and monitor for boxwood leafminer and, in humid regions, boxwood blight.

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil with some afternoon shade; the white-edged foliage of this variegated English boxwood cultivar scorches more readily than green forms in strong reflected sun, so site it out of the hottest afternoon exposure.

directions: Argenteo-variegata is an older English boxwood sport prized for its irregular creamy-white leaf margins, which brighten shaded corners and mixed borders where an all-green boxwood would disappear into the background. Growth is slower and slightly less vigorous than green-leaved sempervirens cultivars, and any solid-green reverted shoots should be pruned out promptly to keep the variegation from being outcompeted. It combines well with dark-leaved companions in formal parterres or as a specimen accent, and unlike the gold-splashed 'Aureovariegata', its cool white variegation reads well against blue- and silver-foliaged perennials. Provide consistent moisture and good air circulation to reduce risk of boxwood blight.

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil; this English boxwood cultivar carries a narrow gold margin around each leaf rather than the interior gold blotching of 'Aureovariegata', giving a finer, more restrained variegated effect suited to formal edging.

directions: Aureomarginata, also sold as 'Marginata', is distinguished from other variegated boxwoods by a thin, consistent gold band along the leaf margin rather than blotched or mottled coloring, giving the shrub a crisp, refined appearance at a distance. It holds its variegation reasonably well in partial shade, though color is most vivid with some direct morning sun. Its upright, moderately dense habit works well as a low accent hedge or clipped edging where subtle color variation is preferred over the bolder gold splashing of 'Aureovariegata'. Prune out any all-green reverted growth and watch for boxwood leafminer and blight in humid regions.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or early fall in well-drained soil; Tide Hill is an extremely cold-hardy Korean boxwood selection introduced by the Arnold Arboretum, valued for its low, flat-topped spreading habit rather than the rounded mounds typical of most dwarf boxwood cultivars.

directions: Tide Hill is a low, wide-spreading Korean boxwood selection that stays noticeably flatter and more horizontal than most dwarf boxwood cultivars, making it useful as a dense evergreen groundcover or low unclipped edging along walkways. Its fine, small leaves take on a bronze-green cast in cold winter weather and green back up in spring, a normal seasonal response typical of the microphylla var. koreana parentage. It is among the most reliably cold-hardy boxwoods available, tolerating harsher winters than English boxwood cultivars while still needing shelter from harsh winter wind and sun to prevent desiccation. Its spreading form also makes it well suited to cascading over low walls or rock garden edges.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil; Morris Midget is an ultra-dwarf English boxwood sport selected for extremely slow growth and small, tightly packed leaves, making it well suited to edging, containers, and small-scale formal plantings.

directions: Morris Midget is an exceptionally slow-growing, diminutive English boxwood sport of 'Morris Dwarf' with tiny, tightly held leaves that stay proportionally small even as the plant matures, making it one of the smallest boxwood cultivars widely available. Its compact, dense habit suits container culture, rock gardens, and miniature parterres where a proportionally small-scale boxwood is essential. It was selected in part for improved resistance to boxwood leafminer compared with older dwarf English boxwood selections, though it still benefits from good air circulation to guard against blight in humid regions. Because growth is so slow, plants purchased small will take many years to reach even modest mature size.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Dwarf Boxwood Cultivars

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in well-drained soil; Morris Dwarf is a compact, leafminer-tolerant English boxwood selection originally found as a chance seedling, slightly larger and faster-growing than its sport 'Morris Midget' but still well suited to low edging.

directions: Morris Dwarf forms a dense, rounded mound of small, dark green leaves and grows somewhat faster than its own dwarf sport, 'Morris Midget', while still remaining considerably more compact than standard English boxwood. It was selected in part for reduced susceptibility to boxwood leafminer, a common pest problem in older 'Suffruticosa' plantings, making it a sturdier alternative for low hedging and edging in the traditional English boxwood look. Its tight branching holds a clipped or natural rounded form well with minimal shearing. Provide good drainage and airflow to minimize risk of boxwood blight in humid climates.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Dwarf Boxwood Cultivars

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil; Wee Willie is a Saunders Brothers introduction selected for an extremely dwarf, slow, dense habit, marketed as a boxwood blight-tolerant option for small-scale edging and container use.

directions: Wee Willie is a very dwarf, densely twiggy boxwood selection introduced by Saunders Brothers, growing into a tight, slow-forming mound of small dark green leaves that needs little to no shearing to keep its neat shape. Its naturally diminutive scale makes it well suited to containers, rock gardens, and miniature knot gardens where full-size boxwood would quickly overwhelm the design. It has been promoted among the newer generation of boxwood introductions bred and selected with attention to improved tolerance of boxwood blight compared with older English boxwood cultivars. Good drainage, air circulation, and avoiding overhead irrigation remain important cultural practices regardless of cultivar.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Dwarf Boxwood Cultivars

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in well-drained soil; Little Missy is a compact, fine-textured dwarf boxwood cultivar bred as a hardier, more uniform alternative to older dwarf selections like 'Kingsville Dwarf' for edging and small hedges.

directions: Little Missy forms a small, dense, rounded mound of fine-textured dark green leaves and holds its compact size and shape with only light annual trimming, making it a popular low-maintenance choice for edging paths and formal beds at a smaller scale than standard boxwood cultivars. It is more vigorous and uniform in habit than some older extreme dwarfs, filling in evenly without the sparse, uneven branching sometimes seen in slower selections. Its dense twiggy structure also lends itself well to low clipped hedges or as a repeating accent in structured garden design. Provide consistent moisture and good drainage, and watch for boxwood leafminer in warmer growing zones.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Dwarf Boxwood Cultivars

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or early fall in well-drained soil; Northern Charm is a cold-hardy hybrid boxwood introduced by Bailey Nurseries, bred to hold consistent dark green winter color further north than English boxwood cultivars typically tolerate.

directions: Northern Charm is a compact, rounded hybrid boxwood bred for exceptional cold hardiness, holding its dense dark green foliage through winter conditions that typically bronze or damage English boxwood cultivars. Its tidy, naturally globe-shaped habit requires minimal shearing to maintain a neat form, making it useful for foundation plantings, low hedges, and mass plantings in colder regions where boxwood options are otherwise limited. Like other modern hybrid boxwood introductions, it combines cold tolerance with reasonably good resistance to common boxwood pests when grown in well-drained soil with adequate air circulation. It provides a reliable evergreen structural element for northern gardens that previously had to rely on alternatives like dwarf arborvitae or holly.
